root.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Variation

sources.title: The Queen's Gambit Declined: Complete Guide
QGD 4.Bg5 / Cambridge Springs / minority attack search summary (Chessiverse, Wikipedia, thechessworld; snippet only)

overview: The QGD with 3.Nc3 develops the knight and adds pressure on d5. The usual continuation is 3...Nf6, after which White chooses 4.Bg5 (pin; Black replies Orthodox 4...Be7, Cambridge Springs, Tartakower ...b6 or Lasker ...Ne4), 4.Nf3 or the Exchange 4.cxd5. Black holds d5 with ...e6, which gives a bulletproof centre but locks the c8 bishop; Black frees the game with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Bb7. White's main plans are the minority attack (b4-b5 against c6) in Exchange structures, or central play with e4. Play is slow and technical rather than tactical, with a strong reputation for soundness, and the Cambridge Springs is the one trappy tactical sub-line.

white_ideas.idea: Pressure d5 with Bg5 (pinning the f6 knight) and decide whether to exchange on d5 or keep tension.
Minority attack: b4-b5 after cxd5 to weaken Black's c6 pawn (a Carlsbad structure).
Develop naturally (Nf3, e3, Bd3, O-O) and prepare the e2-e4 central push at the right moment, or a kingside assault with the centre held.
Exchange Variation (4.cxd5) gains central space and an imbalanced structure; Black gets a queenside majority.

black_ideas.idea: Support d5 with ...e6, then solve the light-squared bishop problem via ...dxc4 and ...c5 or ...b6 with ...Bb7.
Free break with ...c5 (possibly isolated or hanging pawns) or ...e5, which need dynamic compensation.
Tartakower (...b6, ...Bb7) is one of the most solid continuations; Lasker (...Ne4) trades pieces to relieve cramp.
Cambridge Springs (...Nbd7, ...c6, ...Qa5) for pressure along the a5-e1 diagonal and a trap on d5.

typical_structures.structure: Carlsbad structure (Exchange Variation: White d4+e3, Black d5+e6 with c6; White queenside pawns versus Black's three).
Classical QGD pawn centre (d5/e6 against c4/d4) with Black's c8 bishop hemmed in; possible isolated queen's pawn or hanging pawns after ...c5.

character.notes: Slow and technical rather than tactical (Chess Lab Academy). Wikipedia: reputation as one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4; Tartakower is one of the most solid continuations. Cambridge Springs and Lasker add tactics. Play is normally steady.

gambit.notes: Black declines the pawn; no material changes hands. In the Queen's Gambit proper the pawn comes back (QGA).

soundness.notes: Very sound: Wikipedia says it has the reputation of being one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4; Chess Lab Academy: one of the soundest defences to 1.d4 ever devised, backed by a century of world champions (Lasker, Capablanca, Tartakower, Carlsen).

structure.notes: Centre pawns stay on d4/d5, locked or in tension; the typical middlegame is a closed or tense centre, resolved by ...c5 or e4 later. Exchange variation creates an imbalanced pawn structure with the minority attack. Black's c8 bishop is temporarily locked behind e6.

approach.notes: A main-line standard opening played at the top level for a century, a world championship workhorse. Not a system against everything; 3.Nc3 is the principal line.

level.notes: Chess Lab Academy: suited to improvers and above, slow and technical rather than tactical. The strategic concepts matter more than forcing theory: minority attack, bad bishop, ...c5 timing. Theory exists in 4.Bg5 (Cambridge Springs, Lasker, Tartakower) but is manageable compared with sharp openings. Studying Black's side.

plan_phrases: pin on the f6 knight with Bg5

description.claim: The QGD with 3.Nc3 is one of the most classical and respected continuations, setting the stage for a rich, strategic battle.
White develops a key piece, controls the centre and keeps all options open, from pressure on d5 to various pawn structures.
It suits strategic players who enjoy manoeuvring and building up pressure over the long term.
description.note: Chess Lab Academy: slow and technical rather than tactical.

common_plans.claim: White: Exert pressure on d5, often with Bg5, and decide whether to exchange on d5 to initiate a minority attack or maintain central tension.
Black: Solidify d5, solve the problem of the light-squared bishop (e.g. via ...b6-Bb7), and prepare counterplay with ...c5 or ...e5.
